questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct pronoun to complete the sentence: Neither of the boys has done __________ homework.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is a singular indefinite pronoun and takes a singular possessive pronoun 'his'. 'Their' is plural and doesn't agree with the singular 'neither'. 'Its' is used for non-living things or animals, not boys. 'Them' is an objective pronoun, not possessive.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about pronouns:

(i) 'Who' is used as a subject pronoun and 'whom' as an object pronoun.
(ii) 'Each' and 'every' take singular pronouns.
(iii) 'They' can never be used as a singular pronoun.
(iv) Reflexive pronouns end in '-self' (singular) or '-selves' (plural).

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — 'who' is subjective case, 'whom' is objective case. Statement (ii) is correct — 'each student has HIS book' (singular). Statement (iv) is correct — myself/himself (singular), ourselves/themselves (plural). Statement (iii) is incorrect — singular 'they' is increasingly accepted in modern English for gender-neutral reference and indefinite antecedents.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the sentence 'The committee gave its report', 'its' is correct because 'committee' acts as a single unit.
Reason (R): Collective nouns take singular pronouns when the group acts as one unit, and plural pronouns when members act individually.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — 'committee' acting unanimously takes singular 'its'. Reason (R) is correct — the rule about collective nouns explains when to use singular vs plural pronouns. The Reason directly explains WHY 'its' is used in (A). Option B is wrong because (R) is the governing rule. Option C is wrong because (R) is correct. Option D is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following tenses with their correct examples:

Column I:
(a) Present Perfect
(b) Past Continuous
(c) Future Perfect
(d) Simple Past

Column II:
(i) She wrote a letter yesterday.
(ii) He has finished his work.
(iii) They will have left by then.
(iv) I was reading when he called.

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: Present Perfect uses has/have + past participle: 'has finished' (a-ii). Past Continuous uses was/were + -ing: 'was reading' (b-iv). Future Perfect uses will have + past participle: 'will have left' (c-iii). Simple Past uses past tense verb: 'wrote' (d-i). Option B swaps present perfect with past continuous. Option C mismatches past continuous with simple past. Option D incorrectly places future perfect with present perfect.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences use the correct tense?

(i) She has been working here since 2010.
(ii) I had went to the market yesterday.
(iii) They will be arriving at 5 PM tomorrow.
(iv) He has completed the task before I arrived.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — Present Perfect Continuous with 'since' for duration from a point in time. Statement (iii) is correct — Future Continuous for a planned future action. Statement (ii) is INCORRECT — 'had went' should be 'had gone' (past participle, not simple past after 'had'). Statement (iv) is INCORRECT — should be 'had completed' (Past Perfect) because it happened before another past event ('arrived').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Everyone must bring their own lunch.
Everyone must bring his or her own lunch.
Everyone must bring its own lunch.
Everyone must bring them own lunch.
questions.correctAnswer: Everyone must bring his or her own lunch.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is a singular indefinite pronoun and traditionally requires a singular possessive pronoun 'his or her'. 'Their' is increasingly accepted informally but grammatically 'his or her' is the traditional correct form in formal English. 'Its' is for non-living things. 'Them' is an objective pronoun used incorrectly as a possessive here.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about tenses:

(i) The Present Perfect tense connects past actions to the present.
(ii) 'Since' is used with a point of time and 'for' with a duration.
(iii) The Past Perfect is used for an action completed before another past action.
(iv) The Simple Present tense is never used for future events.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — Present Perfect links past to present ('I have lived here...'). Statement (ii) is correct — 'since Monday' (point), 'for three days' (duration). Statement (iii) is correct — Past Perfect for the earlier of two past events. Statement (iv) is INCORRECT — Simple Present IS used for scheduled future events ('The train leaves at 6 PM tomorrow').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct form: By the time we reach the station, the train __________.
questions.explanation: Future Perfect ('will have left') is used for an action that will be completed before a specific future time/event. 'Will leave' is Simple Future — doesn't convey completion before arrival. 'Has left' is Present Perfect — wrong time reference. 'Had left' is Past Perfect — wrong for a future scenario.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 'Whom' should be used in the sentence 'To whom did you give the book?'
Reason (R): After prepositions (to, for, with, by), the objective case 'whom' is required, not the subjective 'who'.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — 'To whom' is grammatically correct. Reason (R) is correct — prepositions govern the objective case, requiring 'whom' not 'who'. The grammar rule in (R) directly explains why 'whom' is needed in (A). Option B is wrong because (R) is the exact rule. Option C is wrong because (R) is correct. Option D is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: If I __________ rich, I would travel the world.
questions.explanation: This is a second conditional (hypothetical/unreal present). In the if-clause, 'were' is used for all subjects (subjunctive mood): 'If I were...' 'Was' is sometimes used informally but 'were' is grammatically correct in conditionals. 'Am' would make it a first conditional (real condition). 'Will be' cannot follow 'if' in conditional structures.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a relative pronoun?
options: The book which I borrowed is interesting.
The book who I borrowed is interesting.
The book whom I borrowed is interesting.
The book whose I borrowed is interesting.
questions.correctAnswer: The book which I borrowed is interesting.
questions.explanation: 'Which' is the correct relative pronoun for things/objects. 'Who' is used for people as subject — not for books. 'Whom' is used for people as object — not for books. 'Whose' shows possession — 'whose I borrowed' is grammatically incorrect in this structure.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following sentences:

(i) She has been living in Delhi for five years. (Present Perfect Continuous)
(ii) They had already eaten when I arrived. (Past Perfect)
(iii) He will be working at 9 AM tomorrow. (Future Continuous)
(iv) We have went to the park. (Present Perfect)

Which sentences are grammatically correct?
questions.explanation: Sentence (i) correctly uses Present Perfect Continuous with 'for'. Sentence (ii) correctly uses Past Perfect 'had eaten' for the earlier past action. Sentence (iii) correctly uses Future Continuous 'will be working' for an ongoing future action. Sentence (iv) is INCORRECT — 'have went' should be 'have gone' (past participle required after 'have').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following pronouns with their types:

Column I:
(a) myself
(b) who
(c) this
(d) each other

Column II:
(i) Demonstrative pronoun
(ii) Reflexive pronoun
(iii) Reciprocal pronoun
(iv) Relative/Interrogative pronoun

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Myself' is a reflexive pronoun (a-ii). 'Who' is a relative/interrogative pronoun (b-iv). 'This' is a demonstrative pronoun (c-i). 'Each other' is a reciprocal pronoun (d-iii). Option B swaps reflexive with relative. Option C mismatches 'who' with demonstrative. Option D incorrectly pairs 'myself' with reciprocal.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct sentence:
options: She told me that she would come the next day.
She told me that she will come tomorrow.
She told me that she will came tomorrow.
She told me that she would came the next day.
questions.correctAnswer: She told me that she would come the next day.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' changes to 'would' and 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day'. The correct combination is 'would come the next day'. Option B doesn't change tense or time reference. Option C uses 'will came' which is grammatically impossible. Option D uses 'would came' — after 'would', the base form 'come' is needed, not 'came'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences correctly use reflexive pronouns?

(i) She hurt herself while cooking.
(ii) They enjoyed theirselves at the party.
(iii) He taught himself to play the guitar.
(iv) I myself completed the project.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Herself' correctly used as reflexive object (i correct). 'Himself' correctly used reflexively — self-teaching (iii correct). 'Myself' used as emphatic pronoun for emphasis (iv correct). 'Theirselves' (ii) is INCORRECT — the correct form is 'themselves'. Options B, C, and D include the incorrect 'theirselves'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The sentence 'Each of the students have submitted their assignments' contains a grammatical error.
Reason (R): 'Each' is a singular subject and requires a singular verb 'has' and singular pronoun 'his/her', not plural 'have' and 'their'.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — the sentence has errors (should be 'has submitted his/her assignment'). Reason (R) is correct — 'each' demands singular agreement. The grammar rule in (R) identifies exactly what's wrong in (A). Option B is wrong because (R) directly explains the error. Option C is wrong because (R) is correct. Option D is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct tense: She __________ in this company since 2015.
questions.explanation: Present Perfect Continuous ('has been working') is used for an action that started in the past and continues to the present, with 'since' indicating the starting point. 'Is working' (Present Continuous) doesn't convey duration from 2015. 'Was working' (Past Continuous) implies she no longer works there. 'Had been working' (Past Perfect Continuous) is for an action before another past event.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the type of pronoun in the sentence: 'This is the man who helped me.'
questions.explanation: 'Who' in this sentence is a relative pronoun — it introduces the relative clause 'who helped me' and refers back to 'the man'. 'This' is the demonstrative pronoun in the sentence, but the question asks about 'who'. 'Me' is the personal pronoun, but again 'who' is relative. It's not indefinite because it refers to a specific person.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the sequence of tenses:

(i) If the main clause is in the past tense, the subordinate clause usually follows in a past tense.
(ii) Universal truths remain in the present tense even when the reporting verb is past.
(iii) 'Said' always requires the reported clause to be in Past Perfect.
(iv) In conditional sentences, the past tense in the if-clause can refer to an unreal present situation.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — sequence of tenses rule requires tense harmony. Statement (ii) is correct — 'The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun' (present for universal truth). Statement (iv) is correct — 'If I knew the answer...' (past tense for unreal present). Statement (iii) is INCORRECT — 'said' doesn't always require Past Perfect; Simple Past can shift to Past Perfect OR remain Past depending on context.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct option: Between you and __________, I think this plan will fail.
questions.explanation: After prepositions (between, with, for, to), the objective case 'me' is required. 'Between you and me' is correct. 'I' is subjective case — cannot follow a preposition. 'Myself' is reflexive — only used when the subject and object are the same person. 'Mine' is possessive — doesn't fit this structure.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following sentence structures with the correct tenses:

Column I:
(a) She writes every day.
(b) They were playing football.
(c) I shall have finished by noon.
(d) He has just arrived.

Column II:
(i) Present Perfect
(ii) Simple Present
(iii) Future Perfect
(iv) Past Continuous

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Writes every day' — Simple Present for habitual action (a-ii). 'Were playing' — Past Continuous for ongoing past action (b-iv). 'Shall have finished' — Future Perfect for action to be completed by a future time (c-iii). 'Has just arrived' — Present Perfect for recently completed action (d-i). Option B swaps Simple Present with Past Continuous. Option C mismatches tenses completely. Option D incorrectly pairs habitual action with Present Perfect.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following uses the pronoun correctly?

(i) It is me who did this.
(ii) It is I who did this.
(iii) Whom do you think will win?
(iv) Who do you think will win?

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'It is I' uses the nominative case after 'is' (linking verb) — formally correct (ii correct). 'Who do you think will win?' — 'who' is the subject of 'will win' (iv correct). 'It is me' is informal but formally incorrect after a linking verb (i incorrect in formal grammar). 'Whom do you think will win?' is incorrect because 'whom' is objective but it's the SUBJECT of 'will win' (iii incorrect).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Complete the sentence: When I reached the station, the train __________.
questions.explanation: Past Perfect ('had left') is needed because the train's departure happened BEFORE the speaker's arrival — an earlier past action before another past action. 'Has already left' is Present Perfect — wrong for a past narrative. 'Already left' (Simple Past) doesn't clearly establish the sequence. 'Was already leaving' implies the train was in the process, not that it had gone.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about possessive pronouns:

(i) 'Its' (no apostrophe) is a possessive pronoun; 'it's' means 'it is'.
(ii) 'Their' is possessive; 'there' indicates place; 'they're' means 'they are'.
(iii) 'Your' is possessive; 'you're' means 'you are'.
(iv) 'Whose' is possessive; 'who's' is also possessive.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement (i) is correct — 'its' is possessive, 'it's' = it is. Statement (ii) is correct — their/there/they're have distinct meanings. Statement (iii) is correct — your/you're distinction. Statement (iv) is INCORRECT — 'whose' is possessive but 'who's' means 'who is' or 'who has', NOT possessive. This is a common confusion.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct sentence:
options: He has been ill since Monday.
He has been ill for Monday.
questions.correctAnswer: He has been ill since Monday.
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a specific point in time (Monday) and requires Present Perfect or Present Perfect Continuous. 'For Monday' is wrong — 'for' needs a duration (for three days). 'Is ill since Monday' incorrectly pairs Simple Present with 'since'. 'Was ill since Monday' incorrectly uses Past Simple with 'since' when the illness continues to the present.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The teacher asked the students to submit __________ assignments on time.
questions.explanation: 'Students' is plural, so the plural possessive pronoun 'their' is required. 'His' is singular masculine — doesn't agree with plural 'students'. 'Its' is for non-living things — not for students. 'Them' is an objective pronoun — cannot be used as a possessive adjective before 'assignments'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The sentence 'I wish I was taller' is grammatically less preferred than 'I wish I were taller'.
Reason (R): After 'wish', the subjunctive mood requires 'were' for all subjects to express unreal/hypothetical situations.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: Assertion (A) is correct — 'I wish I were' is the preferred formal construction. Reason (R) is correct — the subjunctive mood after 'wish' requires 'were' regardless of the subject. The grammar rule (R) directly explains (A). Option B is wrong because (R) is the very rule that governs (A). Option C is wrong because (R) is correct. Option D is wrong because (A) is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences are in the Future Continuous tense?

(i) I will be waiting for you at the gate.
(ii) She will have completed the course by June.
(iii) They will be flying to London at this time tomorrow.
(iv) He will write the exam next week.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Will be waiting' — Future Continuous (will be + -ing) (i correct). 'Will be flying' — Future Continuous (will be + -ing) (iii correct). 'Will have completed' — Future PERFECT, not Continuous (ii incorrect). 'Will write' — Simple Future, not Continuous (iv incorrect). Only (i) and (iii) use the will be + verb-ing structure.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Choose the correct pronoun: The prize was shared between Ram and __________.
questions.explanation: 'Between' is a preposition that requires the objective case. 'Him' is the objective form of 'he'. 'He' is nominative/subjective — cannot follow a preposition. 'Himself' is reflexive — only used when Ram and the subject are the same person. 'His' is possessive — doesn't fit the structure 'between A and B'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Identify the INCORRECT sentence:
options: They have been waiting since morning.
He will come if you invite him.
We had finished eating before they arrived.
questions.explanation: 'She don't know' is incorrect — third person singular requires 'doesn't': 'She doesn't know the answer.' 'They have been waiting since morning' is correct Present Perfect Continuous. 'He will come if you invite him' is correct first conditional. 'We had finished eating before they arrived' is correct Past Perfect for sequenced past events.
